{{Recipe summary
| Category = Chili recipes
| Servings = 6–8
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|Cuisine of the United States]] | [[Cookbook:Texas cuisine|Texas cuisine]]

The '''original Texas-style chili''' version of [[Cookbook:chili con carne|chili con carne]] contains no [[Cookbook:Vegetable|vegetables]] at all, except [[Cookbook:Chili Pepper|chili peppers]]. If using fresh peppers, they should have been prepared by being [[Cookbook:Boiling|boiled]], peeled, and chopped. If using dried peppers, they need to be soaked in hot water for 1 hour before being chopped.

==Ingredients==
*3 [[Cookbook:Pound|lbs]] (1.3 {{kg}}) [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]] or other [[Cookbook:Meat|meat]]
*2 [[Cookbook:Ounce|oz]] (55 {{g}}) [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]] kidney [[Cookbook:Suet|suet]]
*4 [[Cookbook:Chiles|chile]] pods, skinned and blistered, or sun-dried chiles
*1 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoon]] dried [[Cookbook:Oregano|oregano]]
*1 tablespoon crushed [[Cookbook:Cumin|cumin]] seeds
*1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
*1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Cayenne Pepper|cayenne pepper]]
*1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Tabasco Sauce|Tabasco sauce]] (optional but frequently included)
*2 [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]] cloves, [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] (or more, to taste)
*2 heaping tablespoons ''[[Cookbook:Corn Masa|masa harina]]''

==Procedure==
#[[Cookbook:Searing|Sear]] beef in a little cooking [[Cookbook:Oil|oil]] (not lard) until lightly browned. 
#Add the seared beef, [[Cookbook:Suet|suet]], and chile pods to a large iron [[Cookbook:Skillet|skillet]] or pot (at least four [[Cookbook:Quart|quarts]]), and enough water (the reserved "pepper water" if you prepared the pods yourself) to keep the meat from burning. Bring to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], then lower heat, cover, and [[Cookbook:Simmer|simmer]] about 30 minutes.
#Take pot off the stove and add spices and garlic. Put back on the stove, bring to a boil again, lower heat, and simmer another hour, keeping the lid on as much as possible. Stir when necessary, but remember that too much stirring will tear the meat. Add a little more water if anything seems seriously in danger of burning (but as little water as possible).
#Take pot off the stove and skim off all or most of the grease. 
#Mix in ''masa harina'', which "tightens" or thickens the chili con carne and adds a subtle tamale-like flavor. Simmer about 30 minutes more, until meat is done. Do a lot of tasting during this time, (1) to adjust the seasoning, and (2) just because a chili cook should do a lot of tasting.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
*Many of the above quantities may be somewhat adjusted up or down, depending on personal taste.
*The [[Cookbook:Meat|meat]] is simply bite-size—traditionally, it was the size of a [[Cookbook:Pecan|pecan]] nut—or coarsely ground, with ½-inch plate holes in a meat grinder as standard. It must always be [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]], [[Cookbook:Venison|venison]], or other mature meats. Stewing meat also works well. Prime beef or [[Cookbook:Veal|veal]], on the other hand, are not suitable for chili con carne, as they tend not to remain solid.
*Many cooks omit the [[Cookbook:Suet|suet]] as being much too greasy, although it does add flavor.
*Ancho or Anaheim peppers are recommended. For an "elevated" flavor, use four pepper pods per pound of meat; for a milder "beginners" version, use only 2–3 pods.
*[[Cookbook:Chili Powder|Chili powder]] is a barely adequate substitute in the original recipe, but it lacks the subtle sting of the pods. A heaping [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] of chili powder is the approximate equivalent of one average-size chili pod.
*Crushed tortilla chips can be substituted for masa harina (this is what Alton Brown did on the Food Network show Good Eats).
